Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: Karim was seventy-eight when the drum ruptured at the commercial complex where his roofer’s crew was working. He was securing the final membrane on the southern slope when the hiss grew into a roar, and the white industrial fumes spilled from the cracked solvent container, rolling down the scaffolding like a thick tide. He remembered the heat against his face and the sharp, acrid taste that filled his throat. When the foreman shouted for everyone to move indoors, Karim had stayed on the roof long enough to watch the vapor cloud drift toward the chain-link fence where the daycare children waited for their afternoon release. He had come to believe then that the air itself had turned against him, carrying something invisible that settled deep in his chest and stayed. In the weeks that followed, Karim returned home to his wife in their two-story house, but the quiet did not bring relief. He was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. His shoulders remained drawn up, his hands restless on the kitchen table, and he woke often in the night, certain the fumes were still circling the eaves. Sleep was particularly treacherous; he would lie awake for hours, listening to the house settle, waiting for the next wave of unease that would keep him from drifting off again. When his daughter-in-law came by to bring groceries and placed a hand on his shoulder, he jerked with alarm, his heart hammering as though the touch itself were a spark. He learned to flinch before the contact, bracing for the invisible sting. The memories did not always arrive the way he was asked to remember them. When his wife would gently ask how he felt during the spill, Karim would stare at the window and find it difficult to access the specifics; the details seemed to slip behind a glass wall. Yet the memory forced its way into his mind when he least expected it, often without any clear picture. Sometimes he would simply feel the full emotional intensity of that afternoon—the sharp panic, the tightening in his ribs—without a single image to anchor it. He was certain that the air had carried something poisonous, and he would watch the sky with quiet vigilance. A score of sixty-four on his clinical screening confirmed what he had been living. These memories moved through his days alongside his daily routines. Children present stirred him most. When he took the morning bus past the elementary school, he would press his forehead to the cool glass and hold his breath as the younger ones ran across the playground, their small voices carrying a faint echo of the day the fumes had swept down the scaffolding. Related news on the television or radio made him turn the dial quickly; reports of factory leaks or chemical weather warnings drew him into the room, where he would sit stiffly until the segment ended. Known people, especially his old foreman who had worked beside him on that roof, carried a quiet weight. When his crewmates gathered at the local diner, Karim would join them but keep to the edge of the booth, listening to their laughter while his pulse remained steady but guarded. Over the months, his avoidance had settled into a quiet rhythm. He stopped climbing the attic stairs as often, preferring to stay on the ground floor where the floorboards felt solid and the air seemed thinner. He continued working as a roofer but shifted to inspecting jobs from the street level, measuring roofs with a tape rather than climbing. His wife noticed how he no longer stayed to watch his grandson practice soccer in the backyard, stepping back to the porch when the ball rolled toward the fence. His hands still knew the work, but his body had learned to stay close to the ground. Karim finally sought help when the sleeplessness began to bleed into his daylight hours, and the unbidden memories grew frequent enough that he could no longer ignore them. What frightened him most was not the return of the spill itself, but the certainty that the exposure had left a permanent shift inside him. He was hoping, more than anything, to find a way to rest without waiting for the next alarm, and to let the people he loved near him without bracing for the touch.
